pages.x: Paris had held out through a winter siege by the Germans, only to see France's new government make a humiliating peace. Its working people, armed as the National Guard, distrusted the conservative assembly. When troops came on 18 March 1871 to take the Guard's cannons from Montmartre, crowds stopped them, and two generals were shot.

The government fled to Versailles, and Paris elected its own council, the Commune. In its 72 days it separated church and state, banned night work in bakeries, let workers take over workshops their owners had left, and pulled down the column in the Place Vendôme as a symbol of war and empire.

Louise Michel, a schoolteacher and poet, fought on the barricades with a rifle and ran a first aid post. At her trial she dared the judges to kill her. She was sent to the Pacific island of New Caledonia, where she taught the Kanak people and took their side, and came home a hero of the left.

On 21 May the army broke into Paris. In the Bloody Week that followed, Communards fought from barricades, burned the Tuileries Palace and the city hall and shot hostages, the archbishop among them. The army shot prisoners by the thousand; the last were lined up against a wall in Père Lachaise cemetery.

Eugène Pottier, a Communard in hiding after the Bloody Week, wrote a poem calling on the wretched of the earth to rise. Set to music in 1888, The Internationale became the anthem of socialists and communists around the world, and was the Soviet Union's national anthem until 1944.

The Commune was crushed, but it became a legend. Marx called it the first government of the working class, and Lenin, it is said, danced in the snow when his own revolution outlasted it. In France it is still argued over, and the wall in Père Lachaise is a place of pilgrimage.
pts: Paris ruled itself for 72 days in 1871
Crushed in the Bloody Week of May
It gave the world The Internationale
